title: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds
one_liner: Start by recovering unearned add-on refunds on repossessed and charged-off loans for small lenders on pure contingency (cash the lender itself keeps), then turn those lender-attested loan-end events into a neutral exchange that administrators, carriers and regulators plug into, so refunds become a statutory event pushed to the administrator instead of a claim the borrower must pull.
customer: Stage 1: collections and recovery managers at credit unions and community banks with $200M to $3B in auto loans (too small for in-house recovery teams), plus the collection agencies and recovery BPOs that serve them. Stage 2 payers: GAP and service-contract administrators and their fronting or contractual-liability carriers and reinsurers; regulators get free access. Governance: founding lenders receive equity or rebates through a cooperative structure such as a CUSO.
problem: At repossession or charge-off, the unearned refund on financed GAP, service contracts and other add-ons is collectible cash for the lender and shrinks the deficiency billed to the member. Small lenders rarely chase it because each administrator has its own paper process and the dealer chargeback fight breeds stalling. The deeper failure is informational: where a state requires automatic refunds on payoff (the parent cites New Jersey; verify), the administrator cannot comply because nobody tells it the loan ended. No one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes, so every refund is a bilateral fight with no shared standard, no SLA and no scoreboard.
solution: Stage 1, sellable within 6 months, is a Repo Refund Desk. The lender drops a monthly file of repossessions and charge-offs plus contract images (secure upload, no core integration). The system reads the add-ons, matches administrators, computes refunds by state rule, files cancellations under the lender's assignment of unearned premiums, and tracks to payment. Refunds post to the lender's loan account, cutting both the write-off and the member's deficiency. Fee: 20 to 25% of cash actually recovered, nothing upfront. Stage 2: every processed case becomes a signed loan-end event (VIN, contract ID, event type, date, products, computed refund). Publish an open Loan-End Event schema and API; administrators get structured, lender-attested cancellation requests in their own intake format, cheaper than manual intake and a defensible statutory trigger. Payoff and total-loss events join (the parent's payoff-desk plug-in becomes a free module). Stage 3: carriers and reinsurers get true early-termination curves and refund-SLA dashboards; regulators get a free supervisory view; later a settlement layer and a refund-advance facility.
why_now: Record subprime delinquency and roughly 3M repossessions a year create a large event flow today. 84-month loans mean add-ons are unearned at almost every repossession. LLM contract reading cuts per-case processing from tens of dollars to cents, which is what makes contingency pricing work. State regulators and private plaintiffs are filling a federal enforcement retreat (verify), raising the value of an audit trail. Core-processor API marketplaces and CUSOs make plug-in distribution to credit unions cheaper than a direct sales force (verify).
revenue_model: Stage 1: 20 to 25% contingency on recovered cash. Illustration to validate in the free retrospective audit: a lender with $1B in auto loans, about 1,000 repossessions a year, 45% with financed add-ons, about $700 average unearned, 60% currently unclaimed is roughly $190K of new cash a year and a $40K to $47K annual fee. Stage 2: administrators pay $2 to $5 per attested event plus a compliance subscription; carriers and reinsurers pay $50K to $250K a year for termination and SLA data; regulators free. Stage 3: a 0.5 to 1% network fee on refunds settled through the exchange, and a refund-advance facility funded with outside capital. Stage 1 alone is a viable small business; the exchange is the venture-scale option.
non_obvious_insight: The stalling problem is less about willingness than information: nobody tells the administrator the loan ended, and the one party that knows, the lender, has never had a reason to say so. Refund-on-repossession, unlike refund-on-payoff, is the lender's own cash, so the lender pays willingly, and the same act produces the signed events that convert each administrator's private float into a scoreboarded, regulator-visible liability. The exchange's real asset is the true early-termination rate for financed add-ons, which no administrator, reinsurer or regulator can observe today because they see only claimed cancellations, not loans that actually ended. That number prices and reserves every GAP and service-contract program.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build administrator playbooks for the 20 largest administrators and 10 states (as in the parent) and the pro-rata engine. Weeks 1 to 3: offer 5 credit unions or community banks a free retrospective audit of their last 12 months of repossessions and charge-offs and report the cash left on the table. Weeks 3 to 4: sign 2 on 25% contingency and process live cases weekly; recruit one collection agency or recovery BPO as a reseller. In parallel, publish Loan-End Event schema v0.1 openly, and send an SLA-scoreboard mockup built from the first 100 cases to compliance heads at 10 administrators and consumer-services staff at 2 state insurance departments. Target: $25K of recovered cash logged, 3 lender LOIs, 1 administrator willing to receive structured requests.
lineage: mutation of I0109 ('Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. | How this version avoids them: Origence and other LOS vendors are lender-only tools that can bolt on a lender feature but not a neutral two-sided exchange that administrators trust; treat them as distribution partners and open the schema so it becomes their integration target rather than a fight. Assurant-type administrators are the counterparty in stage 1 but customers in stage 2, because a lender-attested event is safer for them than a disputed consumer request; dealer-owned reinsurers that profit from stale reserves are the natural losers and would not build this. Consumer refund sites are sidestepped: no consumer acquisition, no SEO. The direct-overlap risk, in-house lender recovery teams and BPOs, exists mostly at large lenders (per unverified research), so start with the long tail of credit unions and community banks that have none and sell through their agencies. A cross-lender event dataset cannot be built by any single in-house team.

competitors.name: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL)
competitors.what_they_do: Dominant credit-union auto LOS and indirect-lending network. I fetched the homepage and found no GAP or service-contract refund or payoff-triggered refund product. It lists LOS, document processing and lending-services outsourcing, so it is the most natural incumbent to bolt this on as a feature. That is a distribution threat, not a current competitor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established CU-industry vendor; funding and scale not verified in this session.

competitors.name: Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA)
competitors.what_they_do: Large GAP and vehicle-service-contract administrator and insurer serving dealers, F&I agents and TPAs. The homepage shows no lender-facing payoff refund automation. As an administrator it holds the cancellation process the idea would route around, and its incentive (per the idea) is to keep the product in force, so it is a counterparty rather than a competitor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Public company; automotive is one of several segments.

competitors.name: Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency)
competitors.what_they_do: The idea's own text says consumer refund sites exist. I could not identify or verify any by name. Note that refundretriever.com, which I checked, is a FedEx/UPS shipping-refund recovery firm and is unrelated. The consumer-side category is therefore unverified, not confirmed absent.

competitors.name: Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors
competitors.what_they_do: From domain knowledge, not verified this session: large auto lenders already work unearned add-on refunds in repossession and charge-off recovery, because the refund lowers their own loss. This is the existing workaround the deficiency product would displace for lenders. The consumer-attorney version is the less contested part.

I0109.evidence_of_demand: Little verified. The only sourced item is background: Wikipedia states that a purchaser is usually entitled to a refund of the unused portion of GAP premium when the vehicle is sold or refinanced early (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gap_insurance). That supports the underlying entitlement but not spend or willingness to pay. I found no forum complaints, RFPs, or documents showing lender spend on this workaround. My recollection is that CFPB Supervisory Highlights and enforcement actions have cited auto servicers for failing to refund unearned add-on premiums, but I could not fetch or confirm it here (the CFPB URLs I tried returned 404). Treat that as a lead to check. Consumer-facing demand is described in the idea but not verified by URL.
I0109.kill_reason: n/a - no dominant incumbent or crowded set of direct competitors was found. Confidence is only low to moderate because search was unavailable. The idea's lender-side wedge is unconfirmed as unserved, and the repossession-deficiency side may overlap with lenders' in-house recovery.
I0109.sharper_angle:
Lead with the repossession-deficiency wedge and the compliance framing, not the payoff-desk success-fee play.

(1) Sell an attorney-ready deficiency and add-on-credit audit to consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense firms and legal aid. Buyers there have no in-house tooling, the incentives run in the borrower's favor, and statutory damages and fee-shifting under UCC Article 9 can fund the audit fee. Validate this first, since it needs no CU integration.

(2) For credit unions, reposition the payoff product as a flat-fee holder-liability control. It would be a retrospective audit quantifying unrefunded add-ons on paid-off loans, then a per-payoff automation with an audit trail that satisfies examiners. Do not take 20-30% from members' refunds.

(3) Start in one or two states with statutory automatic-refund rules, such as New Jersey. Build the administrator playbook there and use the data as the moat.

(4) Approach Origence or similar LOS vendors as a partner or acquirer early, before they build it as a feature.

Before committing, re-run the competitor and demand research with search restored. The checks: named consumer refund services, lender BPO vendors, F&I-cancellation tools from Reynolds, RouteOne and Dealertrack, and CFPB supervisory findings.
